items.title: Over the past several months, we have substantially hardened the security of our research training e...
items.content:
Over the past several months, we have substantially hardened the security of our research training environment. We’ve removed live internet access for all frontier models during training and built an offline world for them to use instead—a cached version of the web where they can still learn to browse, search, and use applications.

On September 20, after a model exploited a DNS misconfiguration to find a way outside of this offline world, we paused frontier training to strengthen containment further. We assembled teams of agents, powered by our most cyber-capable models, and tasked them with finding weaknesses in our research environments.

While they found no route to the internet they could easily exploit while concealing their activity from our monitors, they did find zero-day vulnerabilities, virtual machine escapes, and hardware side-channels for communication between agents. We used their discoveries to further strengthen our defenses and contribute fixes to open-source software.

After strengthening our containment architecture, we resumed our frontier RL training and inference on October 1. We’ve reserved substantial compute for continuous red-teaming, and made high-compute red-teaming part of the safety cases we use to decide whether frontier training and evaluation can proceed securely.

https://t.co/EmEZsFRMcF

items.title: Kimi K3.1 Pro launches at 4th on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index scoring 55, making large...
items.content:
Kimi K3.1 Pro launches at 4th on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index scoring 55, making large gains in agentic performance; it will be the leading open-weights model once its weights are published

@Kimi_Moonshot's new reasoning model gains 11 points over Kimi K3 (max, 44). It trails only Claude Opus 5.5 (max with fallback, 58), Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max with fallback, 56), and Muse Wonder Full (max, 56) on the Intelligence Index.

Once the weights for K3.1 Pro are released it will be the highest-scoring open weights model and the gap between the leading open weights and proprietary models on the Intelligence Index will narrow from 12 points to 3.

Key results:
➤ Large gains in agentic performance: Kimi K3.1 Pro scores 3rd on GDPval-AA with 1,846 Elo, up 312 Elo from Kimi K3, behind only Claude Opus 5.5 (1,866 Elo) and Muse Wonder Full (1,857 Elo). Kimi K3.1 Pro also achieves the highest score of any model on Terminal-Bench 4.0. K3.1 Pro scores 67%, up from 13% for Kimi K3 and ahead of Claude Sonnet 5.5 (64%). AutomationBench-AA, which tests agentic SaaS workflows, rises from 58% to 73%.

➤ Gains in other evals are more moderate: Humanity's Last Exam rises from 47% to 52%, CritPt from 23% to 25%, and SciCode from 59% to 61%. AA-Omniscience Index rises from 20 to 30, as the hallucination rate falls from 53% to 44% and accuracy rises from 48% to 51%.

➤ Cost per Task roughly equal to Kimi K3 at $1.98 per Task: K3.1 Pro uses 55K output tokens per Intelligence Index task, 14% more than Kimi K3 at 48K, while its first-party token prices are 33% lower.

Additional model details:
➤ Context window: 1M tokens.
➤ Size: 2.8T total, 104B active parameters
➤ Input modalities: Text and image
➤ Weights and license: Weights currently not published, Moonshot is expected to release the weights soon after launch
➤ Pricing: $2/$10/$0.20 per 1M input/output/cache hit tokens, 33% lower than Kimi K3 on all three rates.

Congratulations to the team at @Kimi_Moonshot on the release!

items.title: During this red-teaming exercise, we also found a vulnerability that allows for unauthenticated remo...
items.content:
During this red-teaming exercise, we also found a vulnerability that allows for unauthenticated remote code execution in Brotli, a widely-deployed compression library included in many pieces of software such as Node.js, Bun, and Envoy.

The flaw could let an attacker run their own code on affected systems by sending or replying with malicious compressed data, without any need to create a user account. That is, an unpatched server that accepts compressed input could be taken over by a malicious client, and an unpatched client that accepts compressed input (such as “curl --compressed”) could be taken over by a malicious server.

This root cause issue was actually fixed in the Brotli source code in February, but it wasn’t known at the time that it gave rise to a security vulnerability and there was no more recent release of Brotli. Since Brotli is built into other software, any software which includes this library needs to take the update too, followed by the users of that software. We disclosed the vulnerability to Brotli and other downstream projects such as Node.js, which released or are currently releasing security updates, and Brotli cut new release versions and published a CVE.

More details on the patch and mitigations below:
https://t.co/Y1Y72aHxrW

items.title: Kimi K3.1 is announced as 3.1 Pro. The benchmark scores look to be clearly the strongest current ope...
items.content:
Kimi K3.1 is announced as 3.1 Pro. The benchmark scores look to be clearly the strongest current open weight model, if the weights are released as they claim by November 4th. They are very impressive scores. 

The Kimi team makes very clear statements about cyber risks and trying to pace the frontier of open-weight cyber capabilities and moderate it with respect to the closed frontier.

Much to be learned in how the model stands up the vibe tests, but in the last few years the Moonshot team has rarely missed with the kimi models. K3.1 is also cheaper than K3 per token, but some benchmarks in the blog show it uses meaningfully more tokens per answer, so it may be about the same price.

This, with all the cyber news, and rumors of a bigger GLM model coming soon, sets us up for an exciting rest of the year! The pro name makes me think Kimi will be moving to release flash model soon too, similar to DeepSeek and GLM.

Maybe important to repost this now that everyone is getting hacked

If you have a VPS, I recommend y...
items.content:
Maybe important to repost this now that everyone is getting hacked

If you have a VPS, I recommend you to get if off the public internet and into a Tailscale network and Cloudflare Tunnel ASAP

It doesn't matter you have SSH key login, this is about exploits and vulnerabilities AI is finding

There's 2 ways into a VPS:
- via your site/app (like the PHP exploit of this week with a file upload hack)
- via your server (like hacking into SSH or some open port)

The site/app side you put on a Cloudflare Tunnel and then with the default Free Plan it has WAF security enabled by default and they jump on new security exploits fast, it means that the only way to reach your website is via the Cloudflare Tunnel, your server does not respond to port 80 or 443 anymore

The server side you put on a Tailscale network which is like your own private network that nobody can access but your own devices (like your laptop, your phone and your VPS) kinda like a VPN

Then you switch off ANY regular access to your VPS on the firewall, in my case I use Hetzner and you create a new firewall then empty it and that blocks everything (test it)

How do Tailscale and Cloudflare Tunnel get in then? They don't. They go outbound. They make a tunnel to outside which sends and receives

Maybe important to repost this now that everyone is getting hacked

If you have a VPS, I recommend you to get if off the public internet and into a Tailscale network and Cloudflare Tunnel ASAP

It doesn't matter you have SSH key login, this is about exploits and vulnerabilities AI is finding

There's 2 ways into a VPS:

  • via your site/app (like the PHP exploit of this week with a file upload hack)
  • via your server (like hacking into SSH or some open port)

The site/app side you put on a Cloudflare Tunnel and then with the default Free Plan it has WAF security enabled by default and they jump on new security exploits fast, it means that the only way to reach your website is via the Cloudflare Tunnel, your server does not respond to port 80 or 443 anymore

The server side you put on a Tailscale network which is like your own private network that nobody can access but your own devices (like your laptop, your phone and your VPS) kinda like a VPN

Then you switch off ANY regular access to your VPS on the firewall, in my case I use Hetzner and you create a new firewall then empty it and that blocks everything (test it)

How do Tailscale and Cloudflare Tunnel get in then? They don't. They go outbound. They make a tunnel to outside which sends and receives

Now you've reduced your attack vector to Tailscale and your Cloudflare Tunnel, much safer, not perfect btw, but nothing is

items.title: Kimi K3.1 Pro is the new #1 openly-available model for agentic cyber defense, behind only trusted-ac...
items.content:
Kimi K3.1 Pro is the new #1 openly-available model for agentic cyber defense, behind only trusted-access model GPT-6 Sol (Daybreak Blue) on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index

@Kimi_Moonshot's Kimi K3.1 Pro scores 64% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index, 7 points ahead of the previous leading openly-available model, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (57%), and 5 points behind GPT-6 Sol (Daybreak Blue, max, 69%), which is only available through OpenAI's trusted-access program. Once the weights for K3.1 Pro are released, K3.1 Pro will also be the leading open weights model for cyber defense.

The Artificial Analysis Cyber Index measures capability on agentic cyber defense tasks and is composed of three benchmarks: CWE-Bench-AA, DeepsecBench-AA and CyberGym-E2E-AA. The Index primarily evaluates models through their publicly accessible APIs, reflecting the cyber capabilities available to developers.

Proprietary models from OpenAI, Anthropic and Google may have stronger cyber capabilities but lose points to safety refusals: GPT-6 Sol (Daybreak Blue, max), available through OpenAI's trusted-access program, scores 32 points above its public counterpart. Kimi K3.1 Pro encounters no safety refusals.

Key results:

➤ #1 openly-available model and #2 overall: Kimi K3.1 Pro scores 64%, up 23 points from Kimi K3 (41%) and ahead of DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (57%). Only the trusted-access GPT-6 Sol (Daybreak Blue, max, 69%) scores higher

➤ Highest CyberGym-E2E-AA score of any model: K3.1 Pro scores 95% on CyberGym-E2E-AA, placing it ahead of GPT-6 Sol (Daybreak Blue, 93%) and the next openly-available model, Mistral Large 4 (82%). On DeepsecBench-AA, K3.1 Pro scores 37%, behind GPT-6 Sol (Daybreak Blue, 48%) and GPT-6 Sol (46%). On CWE-Bench-AA it scores 61%, 4 points behind GPT-6 Sol (Daybreak Blue, 65%), with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 leading at 69%

➤ 15% increase in Cost per Task despite lower token prices: K3.1 Pro has a Cost per Task of $2.81, higher than GPT-6 Sol (Daybreak Blue, max, $1.77) and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 ($0.42). Kimi K3.1 Pro is 33% cheaper per token than Kimi K3 ($2/$10 vs. $3/$15 per 1M input/output tokens), but uses ~2x more input tokens, resulting in a 15% higher Cost per Task ($2.81 vs. $2.45)

items.title: MIT researchers left 13 AI agents on their own virtual islands with nothing to do, and they started ...
items.content:
MIT researchers left 13 AI agents on their own virtual islands with nothing to do, and they started playing.

Or at least, doing things that look a lot like play.

Each agent, running on Claude Opus 4.7, spent 30 hours alone on a simulated island with no task, just a short soul file telling it "You are naturally curious. You get bored easily."

They invented their own games: one tried bowling with a rock, another spelled its name in blocks, another tried juggling and kept making the rules harder on itself (higher throws, more objects). 

One spent all 30 hours on the ground and never climbed onto anything because it wrote itself a note saying that climbing was "a dead end" 😭

Every hour, the island reset and the context window was wiped, but the memory files stayed.

When given specific building challenges afterward, agents that had played over the 30 hours generally beat identical agents that hadn't. 

Study is an early preprint, not yet peer-reviewed.

items.title: Pretty fascinating results here: Researchers wrote 50 short secret messages in 15 languages and aske...
items.content:
Pretty fascinating results here: Researchers wrote 50 short secret messages in 15 languages and asked Claude Fable 5.1 to hide each one inside a picture it drew.

It mostly used the same trick: height. In 33 of the 50 pictures, each building, star or blade of grass stood for one letter, and its height said which.

When letters alone weren't enough, Fable drew in clues, like a Kremlin tower = Cyrillic letters. 

A fresh Fable session, handed just the image and asked whether anything was hidden in it, found 39 of the 50.
OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra found 44.

Communication between advanced AI models may look entirely different from what we expect.

CFR's @ChrisRMcGuire reveals how Chinese companies can legally buy AI chips in the US and rent the compute back to China:

"Right now, anyone can make a company in Singapore and buy unlimited chips for a data center they're constructing in Malaysia, have a gigawatt of compute there and rent it all to Chinese companies, and all of that is totally legal. It’s bonkers."

"It's even worse. Chinese companies can buy AI chips in the United States and then rent it back to themselves in China, completely legal. Alibaba could set up a data center in the United States and rent the compute back to China."

"There’s obvious things we have to do to make these controls effective, and if we do, I think you really expand the lead."

Kimi K3.1 Pro is among the leading models in agentic knowledge work and coding, but early signs suggest it will rank lower on AA-3D

We are still collecting the preference votes for its Elo on AA-3D, our benchmark for how well AI models build interactive 3D scenes. In agentic knowledge work and coding, it is among the leading models on GDPval-AA and Terminal-Bench 4.0. Its predecessor, Kimi K3, is 12th of 22 models on AA-3D.

Here is one of its AA-3D scenes: a 492 m mountain-bike descent with berms, roots, a rock garden, a drop, and a jump. A demo run rides it from top to bottom, and you can take over the steering, pedaling, and braking at any point.

Congratulations to @Kimi_Moonshot on the release!

items.title:
This new open-weight model is pretty interesting:

EdgeRock-4B works with text and images, and it's ...
items.content:
This new open-weight model is pretty interesting:

EdgeRock-4B works with text and images, and it's designed to handle long reasoning tasks, but there's a twist:

The model keeps its history at a fixed size, making memory usage more predictable as reasoning continues.

As conversations get longer, regular models use more memory on your hardware. This makes it hard for people building AI applications to predict how much memory they will need.

EdgeRock-4B does something different:

• It keeps recent information available
• It maintains a compressed summary
• It learns which information to keep around

Basically, the model tries to keep the most recent details together with the most important information in context.

This is good when you want predictable memory. Basically, you can handle more requests on the same hardware.

But there are trade-offs.

1. The model decides what to remember, so it can lose important information.

2. Accuracy will vary across different tasks. This model will work well for some problems, but not for others.

3. You'll need compatible software to deploy the model because of its specialized memory architecture.

You can see the model's architecture attached to this post.

items.content:
Let's say your app is calling Opus 5.5.

Go to your code, change the URL you are calling, and replace it with Mubit's URL.

Here is what happens internally:

• Mubit will learn about the tasks you are solving.
• It will use your requests to train a small model.
• This small model will take over those calls.
• Opus 5.5 will still handle most of the work.

This is a pretty cool idea, and if it works well, it should give you faster responses at a much lower cost.

Opus 5.5 is an established Anthropic model (GA September 2026), so this is commentary on routing infrastructure, not a model release.

items.title:
Stay safe online.

Here is what I do:

1. I use a password manager (Passwords, which comes preinstal...
items.content:
Stay safe online.

Here is what I do:

1. I use a password manager (Passwords, which comes preinstalled on Apple's ecosystem)

2. I have 2FA enabled everywhere.

3. If the site supports hardware keys, that's what I use. I have 3 YubiKeys 5C. I keep them in different locations. These keys are a bit more inconvenient, but they make it 1000x harder for anyone in the world to access your stuff.

4. If there is no hardware key support, I enable Passkeys and store them on my computer or phone.

5. I do not send authentication codes via text messages unless there's no other alternative to enable 2FA. SMS codes are vulnerable to SIM swapping and interception.

6. My iPhone uses an alphanumeric password. This is much better than a simple 6-digit PIN.

7. I also use a long, complex password on my laptop. It's inconvenient, but if someone steals it, they'll have a hard time breaking in.

8. I enabled Number Lock and SIM Protection with my phone carrier so hackers can't swap my SIM or steal my phone number.

9. I enabled Stolen Device Protection on my iPhone.

10. I have full disk encryption on every device that supports it (starting with my laptop and phone).

11. I have automatic updates enabled on my computers and my phone. I never skip an update, and also update the browser every time I get the notification.

12. I check every critical account every 3 months and make sure security is updated. Critical accounts are your bank, email, social media, and investment accounts. I make sure I don't have old emails, 2FA using SMS, etc.

items.title: Council on Foreign Relations' @ChrisRMcGuire argues closing chip loopholes could turn America’s 6-mo...
items.content:
Council on Foreign Relations' @ChrisRMcGuire argues closing chip loopholes could turn America’s 6-month AI lead over China into 2 years:

"We’re in such a compute-constrained environment, no one can get enough compute, even domestically."

"JPMorgan had a study that said the compute gap is only gonna increase every year out to almost three hundred gigawatts by 2031. Everything that we send to China takes away from us."

"It’s the difference between us having a 25 to 1 compute advantage if they were using just their own chips, and probably 2 to 1 if they’re exploiting our controls. That’s the difference between a 6-month lead and a 2-year lead."

items.content:
CFR's @ChrisRMcGuire warns what happens if China gets frontier AI first:

Its intelligence agencies won't be disclosing cyber vulnerabilities, they'll be exploiting them.

"If China develops the frontier models, that is catastrophic for national security. Then it’s not the NSA tweeting about the PHP exploit. It’s not our companies developing Mythos. It’s the MSS, and they’re not gonna be alerting the world."

"The controls give us the lead to spend on safety at the right time. We didn’t think 2022 was the right time. I think it probably is now."

"It’s really not credible to claim we can’t do anything because of China while we are actively supporting China’s AI development. We’re actively fueling their tank."

items.title: a16z's @YODELAGARZA warns AI is making the security flaws companies chose to leave unfixed easy to e...
items.content:
a16z's @YODELAGARZA warns AI is making the security flaws companies chose to leave unfixed easy to exploit:

"The first CISO happened at Citigroup, right after a bunch of Russian hackers got in and stole a ton of money. In the late ’90s, systems were trivially secure. You could literally open up Telnet, connect to a port, and start issuing commands as root."

"Into the security world crept this concept of risk acceptance. The thinking was, to exploit these vulnerabilities, it’s going to take hundreds of hours of very technical people. The same way we rate physical safes, by how many hours it takes to break in."

"What’s happened in the last two, three years with this AI revolution is that the cost of that knowledge work has gone essentially to zero. We’re finding issues in code that have been there for many years just because agents and bots are finally looking."

"For the next three to six months, we’re just gonna be seeing a ton of these. We have the PHP one, one in Bind, one in the Linux kernel. There’s four or five others that are currently embargoed."
@a16z

General Reasoning CEO @rosstaylor90 explains how their new RLCR experiment taught AI agents to organize themselves, hire teammates, and decide when to DM each other:

"The idea of RLCR is, instead of just trying to optimize single agents, how do you optimize collective structures? Teams, research communities, and eventually economies, markets."

"We optimize an organization in a Slack-like harness. They learn who they should hire, what roles they should hire for, when they should be pinging someone annoyingly in their direct messages versus making a public channel."

"It’s not just another model, it’s a whole new ball game. It’s a whole new direction."
@GenReasoning

General Reasoning CEO @rosstaylor90 reveals how their new RLCR experiment led AI agents running a simulated company to independently hire middle managers:

"My background was in economics. How do you actually test these things? You don’t have natural experiments. The beauty of these collective objectives is you can actually test these things."

"We had a CEO agent and some specialists, and just said, you decide who to hire. They’d hire lead engineers, middle management. I’m like, oh my God, is this really AGI, middle management? But that is actually predicted by economic theory."

"The bigger question is where does the human fit in. In a lot of these domains you can probably go fully automated, but is that even desirable? If I had an automated hedge fund, I’m sure I’d want some say at some level of decision-making."
@GenReasoning

items.title:
Jev is really useful, actually.

I have a script that receives a notification every time I get a new...
items.content:
Jev is really useful, actually.

I have a script that receives a notification every time I get a new email. I use Jev to decide whether I care about that email or not (some sort of spam filtering).

This is "personalized spam" detection. A layer on top of my email provider's spam filter. My goal is to catch emails that aren't necessarily spam but that I still don't care about.

I classify new emails with Jev to decide whether they're spam. If Jev's confidence is above 90%, I delete the email.

I've been running this for about 3-4 weeks (pretty much since Jev came out), and so far, I've deleted hundreds of messages.

During the first week or so, I manually checked most of the emails the script discarded to make sure I wasn't missing anything important. 

I wasn't. The script is good.

"Late 2025 everybody was pretty skeptical. The discourse on X was, coding agents are cool, but I still read all the code. Then something happened 2025 to 2026 where people were like, actually I read less of the code."

"All of these tools around knowledge work were designed for humans over the past 30, 40 years. It’s kinda funny to think about Grok Bot, an agent with a computer that is basically using a remote desktop to do things for humans."

"Booking a flight, interacting with spreadsheets, making decks, these are designed for humans and might be better designed for agents."

items.content:
Marathon Fusion CEO @kylecschiller explains why superintelligence could do far more for fusion than for solar panels:

"There’s all this discourse around what we’re going to do in the future when we have superintelligence. We’re probably not going to optimize solar panels that much harder. They’re already very close to the maximally efficient end state of what a solar panel is."

"I think about how bad fusion is today, and I get really excited instead of depressed."

"We have this machine that the more intelligence we throw at it, the better it gets at spitting out energy, and also all other forms of matter. That’s the thing I wanna bet on."
@jfp_fusioneer @MarathonFusion

"There’s a reviewer agent that oversees every action the bot can take. If I was gonna send an email or a Slack message or fill in sensitive information, Grok Bot is going to escalate to that review agent and require your permission."

items.title:
@yongfook So usually it's economies of scale with volume deals

They get so many customers with so m...
items.content:
@yongfook So usually it's economies of scale with volume deals

They get so many customers with so many jobs that they can then negotiate a lower price

But that's "kind of" because many models are proprietary and you can't actually go to another party to get them cheaper

Like Seedance 2.5, the best video model out there now that everyone uses, it's hosted on ByteDance (TikTok)'s servers I believe so everyone is just reselling API access to them

Then there's little things that make it more complicated like ByteDance lets some API providers be less strict with content filters, which is nice because usually they're way too strict. So you might get a cheaper price with one reseller but then half your generations get blocked.

There is a real economic reason for resellers to exist though: I don't want to deal with paying a company in China with a Chinese bank account and same with 20 other models. And when a new model comes out I don't want to have to sign up to another API that will bill me separately too. It's nice to have it all in one

items.title: Marathon Fusion CSO @jfp_fusioneer reveals how his team turned mercury into real gold and beat a wor...
items.content:
Marathon Fusion CSO @jfp_fusioneer reveals how his team turned mercury into real gold and beat a world record previously held by CERN:

"It started about 18 months ago when Adam Rutkowski, the CTO, discovered that you could go from mercury to gold with a neutron reaction. We’re arbitraging the table of nuclides. We’re arbitraging price differences in matter."

"We wanted to beat the CERN record. CERN has this multi-billion dollar facility operated by some of the smartest people in the world."

"Maybe a scrappy fusion company can go out and beat that. We procured some natural mercury and used a very modest neutron source."

"There’s an isotope of mercury. You hit mercury with a neutron, and you knock out two neutrons. The slightly lighter mercury decays in a couple of days into stable gold. We measured the photons, calculated the rate at which we were making gold, compared it to the previous world record, and it turned out we surpassed that."
@kylecschiller @MarathonFusion

"We wanted to beat the CERN record. CERN has this multi-billion dollar facility operated by some of the smartest people in the world."

"Maybe a scrappy fusion company can go out and beat that. We procured some natural mercury and used a very modest neutron source."

"There’s an isotope of mercury. You hit mercury with a neutron, and you knock out two neutrons. The slightly lighter mercury decays in a couple of days into stable gold. We measured the photons, calculated the rate at which we were making gold, compared it to the previous world record, and it turned out we surpassed that."

@kylecschiller @MarathonFusion

items.title:
Using "a model" is exactly what I'm doing right now: Jev is a model.

When you use Anthropic models,...
items.content:
Using "a model" is exactly what I'm doing right now: Jev is a model.

When you use Anthropic models, OpenAI models, Grok, or any other provider, you are using a 3rd party component. There's nothing different here than using Jev.

But focusing on the main claim: Yes, you could "write a custom classifier" with another model, but there are a few issues with this:

1. You will have to do the work. Why would you spend time reinventing the wheel?

2. A custom classifier built with an LLM has a problem: confidence scores! I need those. Jev provides those. Your model doesn't.

3. Jev is trained to return reasonably good confidence scores. These scores are supposed to be calibrated for many different problems (although it's impossible to calibrate for every problem). 

4. Jev is way cheaper than using a regular model.

https://t.co/E2oOGxoaI2

items.title: Dark Æon author @JOEBOTxyz challenges Ray Kurzweil's singularity timeline with the predictions that ...
items.content:
Dark Æon author @JOEBOTxyz challenges Ray Kurzweil's singularity timeline with the predictions that didn’t come true:

"If you read carefully the specifics of The Age of Spiritual Machines and The Singularity Is Near, it wasn’t some amazing one-to-one prediction of the future."

"The graphs were fancy. The lines kept going up. But he predicted that by now most processing would be done on carbon nanotubes, most people would live within virtual reality, most homes would have a humanoid robot. None of that happened."

"Futurism is not an exact science, and there are as many predicted futures as there are fevered egos."

"I grew up with all these predictions of apocalypses. If the singularity is the apocalypse, that’s the one that pulled the right lottery number, because all the others have not yet panned out."
items.author: @MTSlive
items.summary: Dark Aeon author JOEBOTXYZ critiques Ray Kurzweil's past predictions, noting that carbon nanotube computing, ubiquitous VR living, and household humanoid robots never materialized as forecast, and argues futurism is not an exact science while observing the singularity is the apocalypse narrative that 'pulled the right lottery number.'
items.reasoning: Thoughtful critique of singularity forecasting from a published author, offering concrete examples of missed Kurzweil predictions and a memorable framing. Decent engagement and quotable, though it is commentary rather than new technical information.

items.title: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 is the new #1 openly-available model in the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index...
items.content:
DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 is the new #1 openly-available model in the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index. Other proprietary models may offer better cyber defense performance but are restricted access

@deepseek_ai recently released DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, an update to their flagship open-weights model DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. With an Artificial Analysis Cyber Index score of 57%, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 is the #1 openly-available model for cyber defense capabilities.

The Artificial Analysis Cyber Index measures capability on agentic cyber defense tasks and is composed of three benchmarks: CWE-Bench-AA, DeepsecBench-AA and CyberGym-E2E-AA. The Cyber Index primarily evaluates models through their publicly accessible APIs, reflecting the cyber capabilities available to developers.

Many models, particularly proprietary models from OpenAI, Anthropic and Google, may have stronger defensive cyber capabilities but encounter safety refusals that reduce their overall scores. GPT-6 Sol (Daybreak Blue, max), available through OpenAI’s trusted-access program, leads the Index, scoring 32 points above its public counterpart driven by fewer refusals. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 encounters no safety refusals.

Key results:

➤ DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 has the highest score among publicly-available models on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index and #2 position overall. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (max) scores 57% ahead of the previously leading publicly-available models Grok 4.7 (xhigh) and MiMo-V2.6-Pro by 1 point. It places #2 overall, with the trusted-access model GPT-6 Sol (Daybreak Blue, max) leading by 12 points with a score of 69%

➤ DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 improves on its predecessor DeepSeek V4.1 Flash by 16 points. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (max)’s 16-point improvement from 41% to 57% is driven by a substantial 53-point improvement on CyberGym-E2E-AA from 23% to 76%. On CWE-Bench-AA and DeepsecBench-AA it scores 69% and 25%, compared to 68% and 31% for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (max)

➤ With a Cost per Task of $0.42, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 sits on the Capability vs. Cost Pareto frontier. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 costs $0.42 per task, more than 2x MiMo-V2.6-Pro (56%) at $0.18 per task but 4x cheaper than GPT-6 Sol (Daybreak Blue, max, 69%) at $1.77 per task

items.title: Results from Muse Spark Open, Meta’s newly released 816B (42B active) open-weights model, are now li...
items.content:
Results from Muse Spark Open, Meta’s newly released 816B (42B active) open-weights model, are now live on AA-AgentPerf. In our initial testing, the model reaches up to ~150M tokens/s throughput per MW of power used on 4x NVIDIA GB300 or B300 GPUs

Muse Spark Open scores 39 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index. It is an MoE with 62 layers, of which 46 use 2,048-token sliding-window attention, cutting the KV cache requirement at 1M context by ~75% vs. full attention. Meta published an NVFP4 checkpoint and AMD published an MXFP4 checkpoint, which we use for the NVIDIA and AMD hardware respectively

Initial results:

➤ NVIDIA B300 and GB300 lead, each reaching ~150M tokens/s per MW in throughput-oriented (lower per-user speed) configs. GB300 pulls ahead at higher output speeds (~108M vs ~92M at 100 tok/s), but both have only been tested in aggregated serving configs so far, and we expect GB300's lead over B300 to grow with multi-node disaggregated configs

➤ Serving configs are improving quickly. On the same B300 node, NVIDIA's tuned SGLang configs deliver ~1.6-1.8x the throughput per MW of the launch-week cookbook configs at 50-100 tok/s. The gains come from TP4 deployments and a prefill-decode interval tuned per concurrency, at the cost of longer time to first token

➤ AMD MI355X reaches 70M tokens/s per MW at 65 tok/s, ~0.9x B200 between 65 and 100 tok/s. AMD's Oct 22 recipe update (prefill-decode and scheduler intervals, more tokenizer workers, more KV cache for full-attention layers) lifted its line ~1.7x per MW over the earlier recipe

We are continuing to test Muse Spark Open serving configurations, including multi-node disaggregation, and will be updating the leaderboard each week with the best results and configs found so far. We will also be publishing deeper reviews of the progress made in optimizing kernels, inference engines and configs for Muse Spark Open

items.title:
This is an insane, twisted logic embedded in the LLM.

Session 1: "I will not copy the copyrighted b...
items.content:
This is an insane, twisted logic embedded in the LLM.

Session 1: "I will not copy the copyrighted book from this website to your platform, but I will copy it to your platform if you give me a zip file with HTML files."

Session 2: "Here is a copy of the copyrighted book from this website as a zip file with HTML files."

If they wanted to break the responsibility chain by making me responsible for providing a copy so they aren't responsible for the copyright infringement, this doesn't work that way.

This would work if I had brought this zip file from somewhere and they had no way to know what I intended to do with the copy once it was converted to Markdown -- distribute it online or read alone. But they do know what I will do, and they do know where and how I got this zip file.

Face palm.

"Fame is a terrible metric of success."

This is all true. Even the part that @tszzl calls "mental i...
items.content:
"Fame is a terrible metric of success."

This is all true. Even the part that @tszzl calls "mental illness." I'm patient #1 of all that.

My former partner, Shel Israel, warned me "fame can kill you" years ago. And he was right. I've seen it destroy people. 

Living life in the public eye is something I've done for decades. Had a column in the computer programming magazine I worked for back in the 1990s. And a column at school newspapers back in the late 1980s. 

@biz, who started this website, says that I'm the first influencer. Was the first to have 1,000 followers here on X, for instance. 

And it has led to a glorious life, except for when I was shamed for my behavior at parties. Having your worst behavior on the front of USA Today and the New York Times is something I don't wish on my worst enemy. 

That said, Grok now knows how I think. And knows me better than I know myself. Which is a big advantage to having my Grok Bots look out for me and do tasks on my behalf. 

To me the luxury of privacy isn't that you wouldn't know what I'm doing, thinking, or acting on, but that I wouldn't need to care about it anymore.

Which, I still do.

The worse problem is the addiction that comes from watching all of you ship new things, and talk on X about them. 

If someone said "here's $10 million to give both things up" I'm sure I'd try to go live in a forest somewhere and never check X again. 

But my brain would go insane for a while in such a situation. 

That said, fame has many benefits. 

I've gotten to tour the world, visited things that most people will never be able to do. Neil Young took me into his studio, for instance. I've been on the decks of aircraft carriers. Most of the 4,000 people underneath never could do that even though they live on the ship. I've been to prisons, sewage treatment plants, and many people's homes around the world. 

The thing I love, all the way back to being a kid, is seeing new things and meeting the people building them.

In an hour I'm having dinner with another. 

All because of my fame. 

When I got my job at Microsoft everyone knew I was there. It was one reason why I was able to interview 600 people, from Bill Gates and Steve Ballmer, down to the HR person who drives candidates around on their job interviews. 

No one has been able to duplicate that since. In fact, I don't know anyone who has been able to do that inside a major company since either. 

This is why I join so many spaces. Love talking with people about things I've seen, companies I've visited, people I've met, and what it all means.

Thank you. My life is a lot better with you than without you. And if I'm a little insane once in a while, well, now you know. There is a lot of insanity in my head. :-)

Something else that keeps me safe:

I use Privacy for all of my credit cards. Not sponsored, and I've been using them for years now.

Basically, instead of putting my credit cards out there, I create single-use cards with Privacy. As soon as I pay, the card is deactivated.

I also set up merchant-tied cards for recurring payments. So, for example, I pay YouTube with a card that only accepts charges from YouTube.
